title: Functors and Natural Transformations

Constructions that turn objects of one kind into objects of another kind, and do so compatibly with morphisms, are formalized by functors.

## <span class="num">8.2.1</span> Functors

:::definition{8.2.1} Functor
Let $\mcC$ and $\mcD$ be categories. A (***covariant***) ***functor*** $F : \mcC \to \mcD$ is an assignment

- to each object $X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mcC)$, of an object $F(X) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mcD)$, and
- to each morphism $f \in \Mor_{\mcC}(X, Y)$, of a morphism $F(f) \in \Mor_{\mcD}(F(X), F(Y))$,

such that

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $F(\id_X) = \id_{F(X)}$ for every object $X$, and
2. $F(g \circ f) = F(g) \circ F(f)$ for all $f \in \Mor_{\mcC}(X, Y)$ and $g \in \Mor_{\mcC}(Y, Z)$.
:::

:::example{8.2.2} Identity and forgetful functors
- Every category $\mcC$ has an ***identity functor*** $\id_{\mcC}$, with $\id_{\mcC}(X) = X$ and $\id_{\mcC}(f) = f$.
- The ***forgetful functors*** $\mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Top} \to \mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Vect}_k \to \mathbf{Set}$, … send a group, a topological space, a vector space to its underlying set, and a homomorphism, continuous map, or linear map to the same map regarded as a function. Both axioms hold trivially. Similarly, there are forgetful functors $\mathbf{Ab} \to \mathbf{Grp}$ (regard an abelian group as a group) and $\mathbf{Ring} \to \mathbf{Ab}$ (keep the additive group of a ring and forget its multiplication).
:::

:::example{8.2.3} The functor $\Hom(V, \cdot)$
Fix a vector space $V$ over $k$. For a vector space $W$, set $F(W) = \Hom(V, W)$. For a linear map $f : W \to W'$, let $$F(f) : \Hom(V, W) \to \Hom(V, W'), \qquad a \mapsto f \circ a.$$ This map is linear, since $f \circ (a + \lambda b) = f \circ a + \lambda\, f \circ b$. The axioms hold: $F(\id_W)(a) = \id_W \circ a = a$, and for $g : W' \to W''$, $$F(g \circ f)(a) = (g \circ f) \circ a = g \circ (f \circ a) = F(g)(F(f)(a)).$$ So $\Hom(V, \cdot)$ is a functor $\mathbf{Vect}_k \to \mathbf{Vect}_k$.
:::

:::example{8.2.4} Complexification
Complexification (Section [7.10](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification)) is a functor $\mathbf{Vect}_{\RR} \to \mathbf{Vect}_{\CC}$. On objects it sends $V$ to $V_{\CC}$. On morphisms it sends an $\RR$-linear map $\varphi : V \to W$ to the $\CC$-linear map $\varphi_{\CC} : V_{\CC} \to W_{\CC}$, $\varphi_{\CC}(v + iw) = \varphi(v) + i\varphi(w)$, of Proposition [7.10.5](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#proposition-7-10-5). The functor axioms are part (c) of that proposition: clearly $(\id_V)_{\CC} = \id_{V_{\CC}}$, and for $\psi : W \to U$, $$\begin{aligned}
(\psi \circ \varphi)_{\CC}(v + iw) &= \psi(\varphi(v)) + i\psi(\varphi(w)) \\
&= \psi_{\CC}(\varphi(v) + i\varphi(w)) = (\psi_{\CC} \circ \varphi_{\CC})(v + iw).
\end{aligned}$$
:::

Some constructions reverse the direction of morphisms.

:::definition{8.2.5} Contravariant functor
A ***contravariant functor*** $F : \mcC \to \mcD$ assigns to each object $X$ of $\mcC$ an object $F(X)$ of $\mcD$, and to each morphism $f \in \Mor_{\mcC}(X, Y)$ a morphism $F(f) \in \Mor_{\mcD}(F(Y), F(X))$ *in the opposite direction*, such that $$F(\id_X) = \id_{F(X)} \qquad \text{and} \qquad F(g \circ f) = F(f) \circ F(g).$$
:::

:::example{8.2.6} Duality
The dual space construction of Chapter 6 is a contravariant functor $\mathbf{Vect}_k \to \mathbf{Vect}_k$: it sends $V$ to $V^* = \Hom(V, k)$ and a linear map $\varphi : V \to W$ to its dual map $\varphi^t : W^* \to V^*$, $\varphi^t(\ell) = \ell \circ \varphi$ (Definition [6.2.9](/notes/math-55a/6-2-duality#definition-6-2-9)). Indeed $\id_V^t(\ell) = \ell$, and for $\psi : W \to U$ and $\ell \in U^*$, $$(\psi \circ \varphi)^t(\ell) = \ell \circ \psi \circ \varphi = \varphi^t(\ell \circ \psi) = (\varphi^t \circ \psi^t)(\ell).$$ More generally, for a fixed vector space $T$, the same computation shows that $V \mapsto \Hom(V, T)$, $\varphi \mapsto (a \mapsto a \circ \varphi)$, is a contravariant functor; duality is the case $T = k$.
:::

Functors can be composed: if $F : \mcC \to \mcD$ and $G : \mcD \to \mcE$ are functors, then $G \circ F$, defined by $(G \circ F)(X) = G(F(X))$ and $(G \circ F)(f) = G(F(f))$, satisfies both axioms. If $F$ and $G$ are both contravariant, the two reversals cancel and $G \circ F$ is covariant: for $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$, $$G(F(g \circ f)) = G(F(f) \circ F(g)) = G(F(g)) \circ G(F(f)).$$ If exactly one of them is contravariant, $G \circ F$ is contravariant.

:::example{8.2.7} The double dual
Applying duality twice gives a covariant functor $\mathbf{Vect}_k \to \mathbf{Vect}_k$ sending $V$ to $V^{**}$ and $\varphi : V \to W$ to $\varphi^{tt} = (\varphi^t)^t : V^{**} \to W^{**}$. Explicitly, $\varphi^{tt}(\xi) = \xi \circ \varphi^t$ for $\xi \in V^{**}$.
:::

:::proposition{8.2.8} Functors preserve isomorphisms
Let $F : \mcC \to \mcD$ be a functor (covariant or contravariant). If $f : X \to Y$ is an isomorphism in $\mcC$, then $F(f)$ is an isomorphism in $\mcD$, with inverse $F(f^{-1})$. In particular, $X \cong Y$ implies $F(X) \cong F(Y)$.
:::

:::proof
In the covariant case, $F(f^{-1}) \circ F(f) = F(f^{-1} \circ f) = F(\id_X) = \id_{F(X)}$, and similarly $F(f) \circ F(f^{-1}) = F(f \circ f^{-1}) = \id_{F(Y)}$. In the contravariant case, $F(f) \circ F(f^{-1}) = F(f^{-1} \circ f) = \id_{F(X)}$ and $F(f^{-1}) \circ F(f) = F(f \circ f^{-1}) = \id_{F(Y)}$.
:::

:::note
Proposition [8.2.8](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#proposition-8-2-8) is a source of invariants: to show that two objects are *not* isomorphic, it suffices to find a functor that sends them to non-isomorphic objects. The forgetful functor to $\mathbf{Set}$ already shows, for instance, that groups of different orders are not isomorphic.
:::

## <span class="num">8.2.2</span> Natural Transformations

There is one more layer: morphisms between functors.

:::definition{8.2.9} Natural transformation
Let $F, G : \mcC \to \mcD$ be two (covariant) functors. A ***natural transformation*** $t$ from $F$ to $G$, written $t : F \Rightarrow G$, is the data, for every object $X$ of $\mcC$, of a morphism $t_X \in \Mor_{\mcD}(F(X), G(X))$, such that for all objects $X, Y$ and every $f \in \Mor_{\mcC}(X, Y)$, $$t_Y \circ F(f) = G(f) \circ t_X,$$ that is, the square

![fig-8-2-1](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-8-2-1.svg)

commutes in $\mcD$. The morphism $t_X$ is the ***component*** of $t$ at $X$. If every component $t_X$ is an isomorphism, $t$ is a ***natural isomorphism***. Natural transformations between two contravariant functors are defined in the same way, with the vertical arrows $F(f) : F(Y) \to F(X)$ and $G(f) : G(Y) \to G(X)$ reversed.
:::

The word “natural” has been used informally throughout linear algebra for maps that are defined without choices. The definition makes this precise: a natural map must be compatible with every morphism. The motivating example is the map from a vector space to its double dual.

:::theorem{8.2.10} The double dual is natural
For each vector space $V$ over $k$, let $\ev_V : V \to V^{**}$ be the evaluation map, $\ev_V(v)(\ell) = \ell(v)$. Then the maps $\ev_V$ are the components of a natural transformation $$\ev : \id_{\mathbf{Vect}_k} \Rightarrow (\cdot)^{**}$$ from the identity functor to the double dual functor. On $\mathbf{FinVect}_k$ it is a natural isomorphism.
:::

:::proof Proof (Let $\varphi : V \to W$ be linear. We must show that the square)
![fig-8-2-2](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-8-2-2.svg)

commutes, i.e., that $\varphi^{tt}(\ev_V(v)) = \ev_W(\varphi(v))$ for all $v \in V$. Both sides are elements of $W^{**}$, so we evaluate them on an arbitrary $\ell \in W^*$: $$\varphi^{tt}(\ev_V(v))(\ell) = \ev_V(v)(\varphi^t(\ell)) = \varphi^t(\ell)(v) = \ell(\varphi(v)) = \ev_W(\varphi(v))(\ell).$$ So $\ev$ is a natural transformation. If $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\ev_V$ is an isomorphism (Theorem [6.2.19](/notes/math-55a/6-2-duality#theorem-6-2-19)), so on $\mathbf{FinVect}_k$ every component is an isomorphism.
:::

:::note
By contrast, a finite-dimensional space $V$ is also isomorphic to $V^*$, but every such isomorphism we have seen depends on a choice of basis (or of extra structure, such as an inner product in Chapter 9). The definition explains why no choice-free version can exist in this sense: $V \mapsto V^*$ is contravariant while the identity functor is covariant, so a family of maps $V \to V^*$ cannot even be compared with morphisms in the way the naturality square requires.
:::

:::example{8.2.11} A natural transformation for $\Hom$
Fix a linear map $\alpha : V' \to V$. For each $W$, define $$t_W : \Hom(V, W) \to \Hom(V', W), \qquad a \mapsto a \circ \alpha.$$ Then $t$ is a natural transformation from the functor $\Hom(V, \cdot)$ to the functor $\Hom(V', \cdot)$ of Example [8.2.3](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#example-8-2-3): for $f : W \to W'$ and $a \in \Hom(V, W)$, both ways around the square give $f \circ a \circ \alpha$, by associativity of composition.
:::
